## Overview

The cassava mealybug arrived in Thailand in 2008 and spread through its
cassava fields. Green lacewing larvae eat mealybugs and can be bred and
released. @Promrak2015 built a cellular automaton of a small cassava field.
Each plant carries the life stages of mealybugs and lacewings, mealybugs
spread to nearby plants and are blown in by wind, infested plants are
surveyed and removed, and lacewing larvae are released. They asked how often
releases should be made. @Promrak2017 drew the same model's algorithm as
flowcharts, which this implementation follows. It is an **adaptation**. The
sources leave out a few rules, and the release sizes they state do not
explain the totals they report.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The model

A 40 × 40 field has one cassava plant per square metre. Each plant is
susceptible, infested or removed, and carries real-valued numbers of
mealybug eggs, instars and adults and of lacewing eggs, larvae, pupae and
adults. Each day:

- within every plant, the life stages follow the source's difference
  equations, and a lacewing larva eats up to 20 mealybugs of each stage. That
  is the model's rule.
- In a sweep over the plants in random order, wind brings instars from outside
  (more often on the two border rows). Infested plants pass instars to
  plants up to three cells away (with probability 0.05, 0.005 or 0.0005 by
  ring), and a plant whose mealybugs are all gone is cleared. Every 14 days
  from day 31 about 60 plants are surveyed, and infested ones found are
  removed.
- While the last survey found mealybugs, 1000 larvae are released (800 if
  fewer than half the surveyed plants were infested), split over the infested
  plants, at the chosen interval.

The sweep and the releases need the whole field, so they are a callback
stored with the problem. It also keeps the field's memory of releases.

```{julia}
prob = problem(:cassava_mealybug; interval=14, seed=1)
keys(prob.kwargs)
```

## A season with releases every two weeks

```{julia}
sol = solve(prob; saveat=5)
counts(s) = [count(==(s), u.state) for u in sol.u]
plot(sol.t, [counts(1) counts(2)]; label=["infested" "removed"], lw=2, xlabel="day",
     ylabel="plants", size=(650, 340))
```

Mealybugs blow in from the first day and spread. Infestation peaks before the
first survey, at day 31, which finds them and starts the releases. The larvae
clear the infested plants within days. New mealybugs keep arriving, so
infestation then rises and falls between about 15 and 110 plants with each
round of releases, while removals accumulate at each survey. The source's Figure 3 shows the same course: about 235 plants
infested at day 30, a sharp fall at the first release, and 20 to 90
afterwards.

## Release intervals

The source compared releases every two weeks, every month and every two
months. Ten runs each, with the estimated yield over the season. A plant
infested for two weeks loses all its yield if this happens in the first four
months, three tenths in the next three, and a tenth afterwards:

```{julia}
function season(interval; runs=10)
    yields = Vector{Vector{Float64}}()
    released = Float64[]
    for s in 1:runs
        integ = init(problem(:cassava_mealybug; interval, seed=s); saveat=10)
        sol = solve!(integ)
        push!(yields, cassava_yield.(sol.u))
        push!(released, integ.p.released)
    end
    return mean(yields), released
end
intervals = (14, 30, 60)
results = Dict(iv => season(iv) for iv in intervals)
plot(0:10:360, [results[iv][1] for iv in intervals]; lw=2,
     label=["every 2 weeks" "every month" "every 2 months"], xlabel="day",
     ylabel="estimated yield (kg)", size=(650, 360), legend=:bottomleft)
```

```{julia}
[(interval=iv, yield=round(results[iv][1][end]), released=round(mean(results[iv][2])))
 for iv in intervals]
```

Starting from 3600 kg, the source's yields end near 2960 kg with releases
every two weeks and near 2915 kg with the other two intervals, about 50 kg
apart. Releases every two weeks agree with the source here. Longer intervals
cost much more yield than in the source, because infestation builds up
between releases. The source's cumulative releases also climb to about 36 000
larvae in steps of about 3000, the same for all three intervals. That is
several times more than here, and more than its stated release sizes of 1000
and 800 explain. The source must have released more, or released at every
survey that found mealybugs whatever the interval, but its text does not
say.

## Larvae and mealybugs

The populations over the field, with releases every two weeks. The source's
Figure 4 shows instars peaking near 220 before the first release and then
between about 10 and 80, and larvae between about 1000 and 3000:

```{julia}
plot(sol.t, [[sum(max.(u.Pi, 0)) for u in sol.u] [sum(u.Mi) for u in sol.u]]; lw=2,
     label=["mealybug instars" "lacewing larvae"], xlabel="day", ylabel="number in the field",
     yscale=:log10, ylims=(1, 1e5), size=(650, 340))
```

The instars follow the source closely. The larvae number a few hundred to
about 1200, fewer than in the source, as the releases here are smaller.
